Sofia, Ben —

High-level legal position and suggested DPA language below. TL;DR: we cannot commit to a guaranteed 24-hour notice when a court order or other legal prohibition (e.g., gag order) prevents notification. Best practice is to promise notice "as soon as reasonably practicable and permitted by law" and to provide operational target windows for routine (non-prohibited) cases.

Legal rationale / principles:
- Compelled disclosures: when Redwood or a subprocessor receives a valid legal request (subpoena, warrant, order) we must comply where law requires. Many jurisdictions impose nondisclosure (gag) obligations.
- Notice: we will provide notice to the Controller unless prohibited by law. If prohibited, we will: (a) challenge the request where appropriate; (b) seek to lift the prohibition if ordered to do so; and (c) notify the Controller as soon as legally permitted.
- Scope & minimization: we can limit production to the minimum data reasonably necessary to comply. Operationally we can produce scoped forensic snapshots rather than full exports where possible.

Suggested redline for DPA (language for Section "Law Enforcement Requests / Compelled Disclosures"):
"If Redwood (or any subprocessor) receives a request from a law enforcement or governmental authority to disclose Customer Data, Redwood will: (a) notify the Customer promptly of the request unless Redwood is prohibited by law from doing so; (b) where not prohibited, provide notice no later than seventy-two (72) hours after receipt of the request; (c) where Redwood is prohibited from providing notice, Redwood will notify the Customer as soon as legally permitted and will use reasonable efforts to limit the scope of disclosure; and (d) when feasible and permitted, Redwood will cooperate with Customer to provide a scoped forensic export that limits disclosure to data and timestamps reasonably necessary to satisfy the request."

Comments on the proposed text:
- I used 72 hours as a pragmatic operational target for notice in the absence of a prohibition. 24 hours is often not feasible when legal intake, triage, and preservation steps are required across providers.
- We should add a clause about costs for extraordinary legal cooperation (e.g., requests that require on-site forensics or repeated manual export) — propose adding an ops/costs paragraph or SOW.
- Cross-border: add that cross-border transfers made to comply with legal process will be done in accordance with applicable law; we will notify Customer and provide available safeguards (e.g., limited export, transfer logs).

If you want, I can prepare a redlined DPA and a short ops note for procurement.

—Kimberly

Adding operational detail to Kimberly's legal framing. This is what we can realistically do and what impacts we should call out to FinReg.

Operational commitments / constraints:
- Intake & triage: upon receipt of a LEA/legal request, security/forensics triage begins immediately (preservation, case creation). We aim to confirm receipt & initial triage to the internal stakeholders within 4 hours; external notice to Customer per DPA target (72h) where not prohibited.
- Scoped forensic snapshot: we can produce a timebound snapshot (metadata + relevant blobs) routed through our forensic pipeline. Typical delivery target for a scoped snapshot is 3–5 business days depending on complexity and whether subprocessors (cloud providers) are directly involved.
- Bulk exports: full dataset exports (if required by the order) can take longer — typically 10–15 business days because of export validation, legal review, egress sequencing, and cross-border checks.
- Subprocessor involvement: when a subprocessor must be engaged (e.g., cloud provider logs, managed DB provider), we will coordinate but cannot compel faster turnaround from that vendor. We will surface the subprocessor name, jurisdiction, and expected ETA to the Customer when possible.
- Cross-border transfers: if complying with a foreign LEA triggers a transfer, we will (a) minimize data transmitted; (b) provide notice where allowed; and (c) maintain transfer logs and audit trail. For certain jurisdictions, sealed handover requests can complicate response; we'll escalate to legal.

Operational asks for the Customer / Procurement team:
1) Confirm whether FinReg expects a guaranteed 24-hour notice — if so, procurement should understand the operational caveats and accept a carveout for gag orders and complex subprocessor coordination.
2) Decide whether FinReg wants a defined SLA for snapshot delivery (e.g., 5 business days) or prefers to keep timelines as 'best effort with targets' given variability.

Attachments I'm adding for reference: forensic_export_spec.pdf (details our format & delivery mechanism) and redwood-incident-evidence-process.xlsx (high-level steps & roles). I'll also draft a short SOW paragraph covering out-of-scope costs.
